opus-5.5.text:
I think the basic case is pretty simple: right now, when we train a large model, we mostly evaluate it from the outside. We look at its behavior on a bunch of inputs and ask whether we like what it does. That works reasonably well today, but it has an obvious limitation. Behavior only tells you what the model does on the inputs you happened to test. It doesn't tell you *why* it does it, and the "why" is what you'd need to predict how it'll behave in situations you haven't tested, especially ones where the stakes are high.

So if you could look inside and find mechanisms you actually understand, like "this circuit is doing this computation, and here's how it feeds into the output," you'd have a very different kind of evidence. You wouldn't just be saying "it seems fine on our evals." You'd be able to say something about the model's internal reasoning.

The case that matters most to me from an alignment perspective is deception, or more broadly, a model that behaves well because it's being watched. If a system is capable enough, it might learn that the way to get a good training signal is to look aligned, whether or not it is. Behavioral evaluations can't distinguish those two cases very well, almost by construction. Interpretability is one of the few tools that could, in principle, catch that. Even a fairly crude version, like being able to detect "the model is representing that it's being evaluated" or "the model believes something different from what it's saying," would be really valuable.

There's also a more modest, practical reason. Even partial understanding helps you debug. If a model has some weird failure mode, being able to trace it back to a specific internal feature or mechanism lets you fix it in a more targeted way than just throwing more training data at it and hoping.

That said, I want to be honest about my uncertainty. I don't think it's obvious that we'll get to a point where we understand large models well enough to make strong safety guarantees. These networks are enormous, and a lot of what they do might not decompose into neat, human-understandable pieces. So I see interpretability as one bet in a portfolio. It's a really important one, because if it works it gives you something nothing else does. But I wouldn't want the whole alignment plan to depend on it, which is part of why I also care a lot about things like scalable oversight and using AI systems to help us evaluate other AI systems. Ideally those approaches end up reinforcing each other. For instance, maybe AI assistance is what eventually lets us do interpretability at the scale these models require.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest version of the answer is that right now we're in this slightly uncomfortable position where we're building systems that are getting really capable, and we basically don't know what's going on inside them. We can look at the weights, we can look at the activations, but that doesn't tell us why the model did the thing it did. And if you're trying to make these systems safe, that's a pretty bad place to be, because you're essentially relying on behavioural evaluation alone — you poke the model, you see what comes out, and you hope that generalises.

The reason I think interpretability is worth pursuing is that it's one of the few approaches that could, in principle, let us get around that. If you can actually find the mechanisms — the circuits, the features, whatever the right unit turns out to be — that are responsible for a given behaviour, then you can ask questions that you just can't ask from the outside. Like, is this model being honest because it's actually tracking what's true, or because it's learned that honest-sounding answers get rewarded? Those two things look identical behaviourally on the training distribution, and they come apart exactly when it matters.

And there's a scientific reason too. Neural networks are weird. They're these artifacts that we grew rather than designed, and we have very little idea about the kind of structure that emerges inside them. Every time people have actually looked carefully — induction heads, the work on superposition, the sparse autoencoder stuff — they've found structure that's more legible than you might have guessed. That's encouraging. It suggests the inside isn't just a big incomprehensible soup; there's something there to understand.

Now, I want to be careful here, because I don't think interpretability is going to be the thing that solves alignment on its own, and I'm somewhat sceptical of the version of the pitch where we fully reverse-engineer a frontier model line by line. That seems really hard, maybe too hard. But I think there's a much more modest version that's still extremely valuable: using interpretability as an additional source of evidence. If I'm trying to decide whether to trust a model, and I have behavioural evals, and I have some understanding of what's going on internally, and those two sources agree — that's a lot better than either one alone. And if they disagree, that's a really important signal that something's off.

So the way I'd put it is: we're going to have to make high-stakes decisions about these systems, and we want as many independent ways of checking our work as we can get. Looking inside is one of them, and it's one that's actually gotten quite a bit more tractable over the last few years. That seems like a bet worth making.

astra-6.text:
Well, we train these neural networks to do well on some set of tasks, but that doesn’t necessarily tell us how they’re solving those tasks. And there can be different ways of getting the right answer that look equally good during training but behave very differently in a new situation.

So if we could understand the mechanisms inside the network, we might be able to distinguish between those possibilities. Is it actually using the reasoning we wanted it to learn, or has it found some shortcut? And, for more capable systems, is there something going on internally that we’d want to know about before deploying them?

I don’t think understanding a few mechanisms would automatically give us a guarantee of safety. But it could give us another source of evidence beyond just looking at what the model says and does. That seems especially valuable when the thing you’re worried about might not show up in your tests.

sol-6.1.text:
The basic reason is that we want to understand why a model does what it does, rather than just observe that it does well on our tests. You can test a model in lots of situations, but ultimately you want to deploy it in situations you didn’t anticipate. And then the question is: did it learn the thing you intended, or did it learn some other strategy that happens to work on your test set?

If we could look inside the model and understand the mechanisms driving its behavior, that could give us additional evidence. For example, is it answering honestly because it’s representing what it believes to be true, or is it choosing whatever answer it predicts we’ll reward? Those can look very similar from the outside.

I don’t think we should assume that understanding individual mechanisms will automatically let us understand the whole system. There’s a big gap there. But it seems worth pursuing because it could give us a way to catch problems that behavioral testing misses, and potentially help us fix them.
